H1.text: Two cyclists leave the same gate. Both end up five kilometres away. Are they in the same place?

H2.text: Not always. One went north east, the other south west. Distance is not enough. You also need a direction.

H3.text: Aarav thought about this on his ride today.

H4.text: He rode four kilometres east, then three kilometres north. How far is he from home, and in which direction?

H5.text: A complex number answers both. How far is the modulus. Which way is the argument.

P2.text: Think of z, a plus i b, as a trip from the origin O: a steps along the real axis, then b steps up, to the point P.

P3.text: Episode forty three builds this map in full. Today, we measure the trip.

M1.text: How far? That is the modulus of z, written with two straight bars around z.

M2.text: Step one. The trip makes a right angled triangle. The base is a, the height is b.

M3.text: Step two. Pythagoras says O P squared equals a squared plus b squared.

M4.text: Step three. Take the square root. The modulus of z is the square root of a squared plus b squared.

M5.text: For Aarav: four squared plus three squared is twenty five. Its square root is five. He is five kilometres from home.

M6.text: And recall: z times z bar is a squared plus b squared, which is the modulus, squared.

G1.text: Now, which way? That is the argument of z.

G2.text: The argument is the angle from the positive real axis to the line O P. Anticlockwise counts as positive.

G3.text: Clockwise counts as negative. We pick the one angle above minus pi, up to pi. That is the principal argument.

G4.text: Watch a trip run. z moves around the origin. Its distance and its angle update live.

G5.text: Below the real axis, the angle turns negative. And z bar, the mirror, keeps the same modulus but the opposite argument.

G6.text: Zero is the only number with no argument. It has no direction at all.

K1.text: Quick one. One plus i, and minus one minus i: same argument, or different? Pause and think.

K2.text: Different! b over a is one for both, but they point opposite ways. Pi by four, and minus three pi by four.

R1.text: So how do we find the argument without a protractor?

R2.text: Step one. Find the reference angle, alpha: the sharp angle whose tangent is the size of b over a.

R3.text: Step two. Use the signs of a and b to find the quadrant.

R4.text: Step three. First quadrant, theta is alpha. Second quadrant, pi minus alpha.

R5.text: Third quadrant, minus pi plus alpha. Fourth quadrant, minus alpha.

R6.text: For Aarav, tan alpha is three over four. Alpha is about thirty seven degrees, north of east.

S1.text: Side by side. Three plus four i, and three minus four i, are mirror images. Same modulus, five. Opposite arguments.

S2.text: Three plus four i, and minus three minus four i, also share the modulus five, but they point opposite ways.

S3.text: Now you try. Is the modulus of three minus four i also five? Pause and decide.

S4.text: Yes! Square both parts: nine plus sixteen is twenty five. A minus sign disappears when you square it.

T1.text: Remember this. The modulus tells you how far. The argument tells you which way.

W2.text: Find the modulus and the principal argument of minus one, minus root three i.

W3.text: Step one. The modulus is the square root of one plus three, which is two.

W4.text: Step two. tan alpha is root three over one, so alpha is pi by three.

W5.text: Step three. a and b are both negative, so z is in the third quadrant.

W6.text: Step four. Theta is minus pi plus pi by three, which is minus two pi by three.

W7.text: So the modulus is two, and the principal argument is minus two pi by three.

X2.text: Find the argument of minus one minus i. Many students take tan inverse of one, and write pi by four.

X3.text: But pi by four points into the first quadrant. Minus one minus i sits in the third. The right answer is minus three pi by four.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In JEE Main and JEE Advanced, on the modulus and the principal argument. And in PUC board exams, on the modulus.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Find the modulus and the principal argument of z. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Root two, and three pi by four.

A2.text: First, one plus i, squared, is two i.

A3.text: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate, one plus i. The bottom becomes two, and z becomes minus one plus i.

A4.text: The modulus is root two. z is in the second quadrant with alpha pi by four, so the argument is three pi by four.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. What is the modulus of minus five plus twelve i?

Y3.text: Two. What is the principal argument of minus one plus i?

Y4.text: Three. Why do z and z bar always have the same modulus?
